docs/guidance/guidelines_v5_2_0_rc6_wiza.old: Start with sm_all, which replaces all working sampling variances with GVF predictions and follows the full-smoothing illustration in Molina and Romero (2025) most closely. Compare with direct when design variances are credible and with sm_out as an optional sensitivity, and document the chosen treatment. Under sm_out, a finite direct variance at least 0.001 is retained; a missing, non-finite, or strictly smaller value is replaced with its GVF prediction. Large direct variances are not replaced. Full smoothing still requires suitable GVF fit and diagnostics.
docs/guidance/guidelines_v5_2_0_rc6_wiza.new: Start with sm_out, the default for new configurations. It keeps each area's direct variance and replaces only a missing, non-finite, or strictly below-0.001 value with its GVF prediction; large direct variances are not replaced. Use sm_all, which replaces all working sampling variances with GVF predictions, only when direct variances are broadly unstable and the GVF fits well. Compare with direct when design variances are credible, and document the chosen treatment.

docs/guidance/guidelines_v5_2_0_rc6_wiza.new: Choosing between sm_out and sm_all. Full smoothing (sm_all) follows the full-smoothing illustration in Molina and Romero (2025) and removes the noise in individual variance estimates, but it is only as good as the GVF. Because the GVF predicts each variance from the area sample size alone, areas with similar sample sizes receive similar variances whatever the value of the indicator. For a poverty headcount, the sampling variance is approximately p(1 − p) deff / n, so it depends strongly on the poverty rate p. When poverty rates differ widely across areas of similar size, sm_all overestimates the sampling variances of low-poverty areas and underestimates those of high-poverty areas. The lognormal correction in Annex G.3 raises every smoothed variance further when the GVF explains little of the variation in the direct variances.

docs/guidance/guidelines_v5_2_0_rc6_wiza.new: Overstated variances have visible consequences. The model gives too little weight to the direct estimates of low-poverty areas and shrinks them too far toward the regression prediction, and their reported MSEs reflect the inflated variance rather than the survey data. MFH RMSEs then look almost constant across areas, and model RMSEs can exceed direct RMSEs mainly where poverty is low. In the two-year Spanish teaching example (Data/Spain_2y), sm_all assigned low-poverty provinces about 2.4 to 2.5 times their direct variances, and MFH RMSEs were below direct RMSEs in 63 to 73 percent of provinces, against 94 percent under sm_out.
docs/guidance/guidelines_v5_2_0_rc6_wiza.locator: Section 6.6, new discussion: consequences and example

docs/guidance/guidelines_v5_2_0_rc6_wiza.new: Because most Workbench applications estimate poverty rates, new configurations default to sm_out. Prefer sm_all only when direct variances are broadly unreliable, for example when many are zero or missing or areas have very few PSUs, and when the GVF fits well. For mean welfare modeled in logs, the sampling variance of the log area mean depends mainly on the sample size and the dispersion of welfare rather than on its level, so the GVF is usually better suited there. Whichever option is used, compare model and direct RMSEs across the range of the indicator: nearly constant model RMSEs, or model RMSEs above direct RMSEs concentrated in low-poverty areas, suggest that full smoothing overstates variances. Under sm_out, direct variances from small samples remain noisy and are treated as known, so individual model RMSEs should be read with care.
